### 2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 6 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">Transformed roots</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The equation

$$x^3-x+1=0$$

has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(i)** Use the relation $x=y^{1/3}$ to show that the equation

$$y^3+3y^2+2y+1=0$$

has roots $\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3$. Hence write down the value of
$\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3$. **[3]**

Let $S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n$.

**(ii)** Find the value of $S_{-3}$. **[2]**

**(iii)** Show that $S_6=5$ and find the value of $S_9$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(i)** Put $y=x^3$, so $x=y^{1/3}$. Then

$$
y-y^{1/3}+1=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y+1=y^{1/3}.
$$

Cubing both sides,

$$y=(y+1)^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y^3+3y^2+2y+1=0. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

The three roots are $\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3$, so Vieta's formula gives $\boxed{S_3=-3}$. **B1**

**(ii)** For the roots $\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3$, the sum of pairwise products is $2$ and the product is $-1$. Hence

$$S_{-3}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(iii)**

$$S_6=S_3^2-2(2)=(-3)^2-4=5. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

Summing the transformed equation over its three roots gives

$$S_9+3S_6+2S_3+3=0,$$

so

$$S_9=-3(5)-2(-3)-3=-12. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2019-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2019, Q6; 9231/12/M/J/2019, Q6.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2019-mj-13}
### 2019 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 9 · 11 marks

<span class="tag">Unknown coefficients</span><span class="tag">Symmetric sums</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

A cubic equation

$$x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$$

has real roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ such that

$$
\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma=-\frac5{12},
\qquad \alpha\beta\gamma=-12,
\qquad \alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=90.
$$

**(i)** Find the values of $c$ and $d$. **[3]**

**(ii)** Express $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ in terms of $b$. **[2]**

**(iii)** Show that $b^3-15b+126=0$. **[4]**

**(iv)** Given that $3+i\sqrt{12}$ is a root of $y^3-15y+126=0$, deduce the value of $b$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(i)** Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=-d=-12$, $d=12$. **B1**

Also

$$\frac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\frac5{12},$$

so $c=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=5$. **M1 A1**

**(ii)**

$$\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2c=b^2-10. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(iii)** Since $S_2=b^2-10$ and every root satisfies $x^3=-bx^2-5x-12$, summing over all three roots gives

$$90=-b(b^2-10)-5(-b)-36.$$

Hence

$$b^3-15b+126=0. \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1 A1}$$

**(iv)** The polynomial has real coefficients, so $3-i\sqrt{12}$ is also a root. These two roots have sum $6$. Since the coefficient of $y^2$ is zero, the third root is $-6$. Thus the required real value is $\boxed{b=-6}$. **M1 A1**

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2019-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2019, Q9.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2019-on}
### 2019 October/November · 9231/11, 9231/12 & 9231/13 · Question 7 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Transformed roots</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The equation $x^3+2x^2+x+7=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(i)** Use the relation $x^2=-7y$ to show that

$$49y^3+14y^2-27y+7=0$$

has roots

$$\frac{\alpha}{\beta\gamma},\qquad
\frac{\beta}{\gamma\alpha},\qquad
\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\beta}. \qquad \textbf{[4]}$$

**(ii)** Show that

$$\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta^2\gamma^2}+
\frac{\beta^2}{\gamma^2\alpha^2}+
\frac{\gamma^2}{\alpha^2\beta^2}=\frac{58}{49}. \qquad \textbf{[3]}$$

**(iii)** Find the exact value of

$$
\frac{\alpha^3}{\beta^3\gamma^3}+
\frac{\beta^3}{\gamma^3\alpha^3}+
\frac{\gamma^3}{\alpha^3\beta^3}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}
$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=-7$,

$$\frac{\alpha}{\beta\gamma}=-\frac{\alpha^2}{7},$$

and similarly for the other two roots. With $x^2=-7y$, the original equation becomes

$$
x(1-7y)+7(1-2y)=0,
$$

so $x=7(2y-1)/(1-7y)$. Squaring and using $x^2=-7y$ gives

$$
49(2y-1)^2=-7y(1-7y)^2,
$$

which simplifies to the stated cubic. **M1 M1 A1 A1**

For the transformed roots,

$$e_1=-\frac27,\qquad e_2=-\frac{27}{49},\qquad e_3=-\frac17.$$

Therefore

$$p_2=e_1^2-2e_2=\frac4{49}+\frac{54}{49}=\frac{58}{49}. \qquad \text{M1 A1 A1}$$

Also

$$p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=-\frac{317}{343}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2019-on"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2019, Q7; 9231/12/O/N/2019, Q7; 9231/13/O/N/2019, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 8 marks

<span class="tag">Squared roots</span><span class="tag">Unknown coefficient</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $6x^3+px^2-3x-5=0$, where $p$ is a constant, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find a cubic equation whose roots are $\alpha^2,\beta^2,\gamma^2$. **[3]**

**(b)** It is given that

$$\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma).$$

**(i)** Find the value of $p$. **[3]**

**(ii)** Find the value of $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=x^2$. Rewriting the original equation gives $x(6y-3)=5-py$. Squaring and using $x^2=y$ gives

$$y(6y-3)^2=(5-py)^2,$$

hence

$$36y^3-(p^2+36)y^2+(10p+9)y-25=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(b)(i)**

$$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\frac p6,\qquad
\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=-\frac12.$$

Thus

$$\frac{p^2}{36}+1=-\frac p3,$$

so $(p+6)^2=0$ and $p=-6$. **M1 A1 A1**

**(b)(ii)** With $p=-6$,

$$e_1=1,\qquad e_2=-\frac12,\qquad e_3=\frac56,$$

and

$$\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=e_1^3-3e_1e_2+3e_3=5. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2020-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q2.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2020-mj-13}
### 2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 1 · 7 marks

<span class="tag">Reciprocal roots</span><span class="tag">Negative powers</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $7x^3+3x^2+5x+1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find a cubic equation whose roots are $\alpha^{-1},\beta^{-1},\gamma^{-1}$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find $\alpha^{-2}+\beta^{-2}+\gamma^{-2}$. **[2]**

**(c)** Find $\alpha^{-3}+\beta^{-3}+\gamma^{-3}$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=1/x$. Then

$$
\frac7{y^3}+\frac3{y^2}+\frac5y+1=0.
$$

Multiplying by $y^3$ gives

$$y^3+5y^2+3y+7=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

For the reciprocal roots, $e_1=-5$, $e_2=3$, $e_3=-7$.

**(b)**

$$p_2=e_1^2-2e_2=25-6=19. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)**

$$p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=-5(19)-3(-5)-21=-101. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2020-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2020, Q1.</div>
:::

### 2020 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 3 · 11 marks

<span class="tag">Cubed roots</span><span class="tag">Singular matrix</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+cx+1=0$, where $c$ is a constant, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find a cubic equation whose roots are $\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that $\alpha^6+\beta^6+\gamma^6=3-2c^3$. **[3]**

**(c)** Find the real value of $c$ for which

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\alpha^3&\beta^3\\
\alpha^3&1&\gamma^3\\
\beta^3&\gamma^3&1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

is singular. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=x^3$. Since $cx=-(y+1)$, cubing and using $x^3=y$ gives $c^3y=-(y+1)^3$, hence

$$y^3+3y^2+(c^3+3)y+1=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(b)** For the new roots, $e_1=-3$ and $e_2=c^3+3$. Hence

$$\alpha^6+\beta^6+\gamma^6=(-3)^2-2(c^3+3)=3-2c^3. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(c)** Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=-1$,

$$\alpha^3\beta^3\gamma^3=-1.$$

The determinant is

$$1-(\alpha^6+\beta^6+\gamma^6)+2\alpha^3\beta^3\gamma^3=2c^3-4.$$

Therefore $c^3=2$ and

$$c=\sqrt[3]{2}. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1 M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2020-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2020, Q3; 9231/13/O/N/2020, Q3.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2020-on-12}
### 2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 1 · 8 marks

<span class="tag">Linear transformation</span><span class="tag">Unknown coefficients</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$, where $b,c,d$ are constants, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. It is given that $\alpha\beta\gamma=-1$.

**(a)** State the value of $d$. **[1]**

**(b)** Find a cubic equation, with coefficients in terms of $b$ and $c$, whose roots are $\alpha+1,\beta+1,\gamma+1$. **[3]**

**(c)** Given also that $\gamma+1=-\alpha-1$, deduce that

$$(c-2b+3)(b-3)=b-c. \qquad \textbf{[4]}$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=-d=-1$, $d=1$. **B1**

**(b)** The transformed roots have

$$e_1'=3-b,\qquad e_2'=c-2b+3,\qquad e_3'=c-b.$$

Thus the required equation is

$$x^3+(b-3)x^2+(c-2b+3)x+(b-c)=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(c)** Write the transformed roots as $r,-r,s$. Their sum gives $s=3-b$. Also their pairwise sum is $-r^2=e_2'$ and their product is $-r^2s=e_3'$. Hence

$$e_3'=e_2'(3-b).$$

Therefore

$$c-b=(c-2b+3)(3-b),$$

which is equivalent to the required result. **B1 B1 M1 A1**

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2020-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2020, Q1.</div>
:::

### 2021 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 3 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Quartic equation</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The equation $x^4-2x^3-1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.

**(a)** Find a quartic equation whose roots are $\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3,\delta^3$ and state the value of $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3$. **[4]**

**(b)** Find

$$\frac1{\alpha^3}+\frac1{\beta^3}+\frac1{\gamma^3}+\frac1{\delta^3}. \qquad \textbf{[3]}$$

**(c)** Find $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=x^3$. Since $x^4=2x^3+1$ and no root is zero,

$$
x=2+\frac1y=\frac{2y+1}{y}.
$$

Cubing and using $x^3=y$ gives

$$y^4-(2y+1)^3=0,$$

so

$$y^4-8y^3-12y^2-6y-1=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

Hence $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3=8$. **B1**

**(b)** For the transformed equation, $e_3=6$ and $e_4=-1$. Therefore

$$\sum\frac1{\alpha^3}=\frac{e_3}{e_4}=-6. \qquad \text{M1 A1 A1}$$

**(c)** Since $x^4=2x^3+1$ for every root,

$$\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4=2(8)+4=20. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2021-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2021, Q3; 9231/12/M/J/2021, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2021 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 11 marks

<span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">Pair sums</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The cubic equation $2x^3-4x^2+3=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. Let

$$S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n.$$

**(a)** State the value of $S_1$ and find the value of $S_2$. **[3]**

**(b)(i)** Express $S_{n+3}$ in terms of $S_{n+2}$ and $S_n$. **[1]**

**(b)(ii)** Hence, or otherwise, find $S_4$. **[2]**

**(c)** Use the substitution $y=S_1-x$, where $S_1$ is the numerical value found in part (a), to find and simplify an equation whose roots are $\alpha+\beta,\beta+\gamma,\gamma+\alpha$. **[3]**

**(d)** Find

$$\frac1{\alpha+\beta}+\frac1{\beta+\gamma}+\frac1{\gamma+\alpha}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** $S_1=2$. Since $e_2=0$,

$$S_2=S_1^2-2e_2=4. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(b)(i)** From $2x^3-4x^2+3=0$,

$$S_{n+3}=2S_{n+2}-\frac32S_n. \qquad \text{B1}$$

**(b)(ii)** Taking $n=0$ in the recurrence gives

$$
S_3=2S_2-\frac32S_0=2(4)-\frac32(3)=\frac72.
$$

Taking $n=1$ then gives

$$S_4=2S_3-\frac32S_1=4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)** Put $x=2-y$:

$$2(2-y)^3-4(2-y)^2+3=0,$$

which simplifies to

$$2y^3-8y^2+8y-3=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(d)** For the new roots,

$$\sum\frac1y=\frac{8}{3}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2021-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2021, Q2.</div>
:::

### 2021 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 1 · 6 marks

<span class="tag">Recovering coefficients</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

It is given that

$$
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=3,\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=5,\qquad
\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=6.
$$

The cubic equation $x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. Find $b,c,d$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

$$b=-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=-3. \qquad \text{B1}$$

Using $5=3^2-2c$ gives $c=2$. **M1 A1**

Using

$$p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3$$

gives

$$6=3(5)-2(3)-3d,$$

so $d=1$. **M1 A1 A1**

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2021-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2021, Q1; 9231/13/O/N/2021, Q1.</div>
:::

### 2021 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks

<span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">Summation</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+2x^2+3x+3=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. **[2]**

**(b)** Show that $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=1$. **[2]**

**(c)** Use standard results from the list of formulae (MF19) to show that

$$
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left((\alpha+r)^3+(\beta+r)^3+(\gamma+r)^3\right)
=n+\frac14n(n+1)(an^2+bn+c),
$$

where $a,b,c$ are constants to be determined. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$p_2=(-2)^2-2(3)=-2. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(b)** Summing the original equation over the roots,

$$p_3+2p_2+3p_1+9=0,$$

so $p_3=1$. **M1 A1**

**(c)** For each $r$,

$$
(\alpha+r)^3+(\beta+r)^3+(\gamma+r)^3
=p_3+3rp_2+3r^2p_1+3r^3.
$$

Using $p_1=-2$, $p_2=-2$ and $p_3=1$, expand

$$\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(1-6r-6r^2+3r^3\right). \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

Using the standard sums and simplifying gives

$$n+\frac14n(n+1)(3n^2-5n-16). \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1}$$

Thus

$$a=3,\qquad b=-5,\qquad c=-16.$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2021-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2021, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2022 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 8 marks

<span class="tag">Reciprocal powers</span><span class="tag">Transformed roots</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The cubic equation $2x^3+5x^2-6=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find a cubic equation whose roots are $1/\alpha^3,1/\beta^3,1/\gamma^3$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find

$$\frac1{\alpha^6}+\frac1{\beta^6}+\frac1{\gamma^6}. \qquad \textbf{[3]}$$

**(c)** Find also

$$\frac1{\alpha^9}+\frac1{\beta^9}+\frac1{\gamma^9}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** First put $t=1/x$. Dividing the original equation by $x^3$ gives

$$
2+5t-6t^3=0,
$$

so the reciprocal roots satisfy $6t^3-5t-2=0$. Now put $y=t^3$. Then

$$
5t=6y-2.
$$

Cubing and using $t^3=y$ gives

$$
125y=(6y-2)^3.
$$

Expanding and simplifying gives

$$216y^3-216y^2-53y-8=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(b)** For the transformed roots,

$$e_1=1,\qquad e_2=-\frac{53}{216}.$$

Therefore

$$p_2=1-2\left(-\frac{53}{216}\right)=\frac{161}{108}. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(c)** If $z$ is one of the transformed roots, then

$$
216z^3-216z^2-53z-8=0.
$$

Summing this equation over all three transformed roots gives

$$216S_{-9}=216S_{-6}+53S_{-3}+24.$$

Since $S_{-3}=1$,

$$S_{-9}=\frac{133}{72}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2022-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2022, Q4; 9231/12/M/J/2022, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks

<span class="tag">Symmetric sums</span><span class="tag">Singular matrix</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+5x^2+10x-2=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. **[3]**

**(b)** Show that

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\alpha&\beta\\
\alpha&1&\gamma\\
\beta&\gamma&1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

is singular. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** $e_1=-5$, $e_2=10$, so

$$\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=25-20=5. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(b)** The determinant is

$$1-\alpha^2-\beta^2-\gamma^2+2\alpha\beta\gamma.$$

Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=2$,

$$1-5+2(2)=0.$$

Therefore the matrix is singular. **M1 A1 M1 A1**

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2022-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2022, Q2.</div>
:::

### 2023

### 2023 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 3 · 8 marks

<span class="tag">Quartic equation</span><span class="tag">Unknown coefficients</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The quartic equation

$$x^4+bx^3+cx^2+dx-2=0$$

has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$. It is given that

$$
\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=3,
$$

$$
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2=5,
$$

and

$$
\alpha^{-1}+\beta^{-1}+\gamma^{-1}+\delta^{-1}=6.
$$

**(a)** Find $b,c,d$. **[6]**

**(b)** Given also that $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3=-27$, find $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$b=-3. \qquad \text{B1}$$

Also

$$5=3^2-2c,$$

so $c=2$. **M1 A1**

Here $e_4=-2$ and $e_3=-d$. Since the reciprocal sum is $e_3/e_4$,

$$\frac{-d}{-2}=6,$$

so $d=12$. **M1 A1 A1**

**(b)** Summing the quartic equation over the roots gives

$$p_4-3p_3+2p_2+12p_1-8=0.$$

Hence

$$p_4=3(-27)-2(5)-12(3)+8=-119. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2023-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2023, Q3; 9231/13/O/N/2023, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2023 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks

<span class="tag">Linear transformation</span><span class="tag">Positive and negative powers</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The cubic equation $27x^3+18x^2+6x-1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Show that a cubic equation with roots $3\alpha+1,3\beta+1,3\gamma+1$ is

$$y^3-y^2+y-2=0. \qquad \textbf{[3]}$$

The sum $(3\alpha+1)^n+(3\beta+1)^n+(3\gamma+1)^n$ is denoted by $S_n$.

**(b)** Find $S_2$ and $S_3$. **[4]**

**(c)** Find $S_{-1}$ and $S_{-2}$. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=3x+1$, so $x=(y-1)/3$. Then

$$
27\left(\frac{y-1}{3}\right)^3
+18\left(\frac{y-1}{3}\right)^2
+6\left(\frac{y-1}{3}\right)-1=0.
$$

Expanding and simplifying gives

$$y^3-y^2+y-2=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

For the transformed roots, $e_1=1$, $e_2=1$, $e_3=2$.

**(b)**

$$S_2=e_1^2-2e_2=-1, \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

$$S_3=e_1S_2-e_2S_1+3e_3=4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)**

$$S_{-1}=\frac{e_2}{e_3}=\frac12. \qquad \text{B1}$$

For the reciprocal roots, the pairwise sum is $e_1/e_3=1/2$. Hence

$$S_{-2}=\left(\frac12\right)^2-2\left(\frac12\right)=-\frac34. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2023-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2023, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2024

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2024-mj-11-12}
### 2024 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 1 · 6 marks

<span class="tag">Pairwise products</span><span class="tag">Unknown coefficient</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $2x^3+x^2-px-5=0$, where $p$ is a positive constant, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** State, in terms of $p$, the value of $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha$. **[1]**

**(b)** Find $\alpha^2\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta^2\gamma+\alpha\beta\gamma^2$. **[2]**

**(c)** Deduce a cubic equation whose roots are $\alpha\beta,\beta\gamma,\alpha\gamma$. **[1]**

**(d)** Given that $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=\frac13$, find $p$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=-\frac p2. \qquad \text{B1}$$

**(b)**

$$\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\frac52\left(-\frac12\right)=-\frac54. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)** The new roots have sum $-p/2$, pairwise sum $-5/4$, and product $25/4$. Thus

$$4y^3+2py^2-5y-25=0. \qquad \text{B1}$$

**(d)**

$$\frac13=\left(-\frac12\right)^2-2\left(-\frac p2\right)=\frac14+p,$$

so

$$p=\frac1{12}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2024-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2024, Q1; 9231/12/M/J/2024, Q1.</div>
:::

### 2024 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks

<span class="tag">Squared roots</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+2x^2+3x+1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find a cubic equation whose roots are $\alpha^2+1,\beta^2+1,\gamma^2+1$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find

$$\left(\alpha^2+1\right)^2+\left(\beta^2+1\right)^2+\left(\gamma^2+1\right)^2. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

**(c)** Find

$$\left(\alpha^2+1\right)^3+\left(\beta^2+1\right)^3+\left(\gamma^2+1\right)^3. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=x^2+1$, so $x^2=y-1$. The original equation can be written as

$$
x(x^2+3)=-(2x^2+1),
$$

hence

$$
x(y+2)=1-2y.
$$

Squaring and using $x^2=y-1$ gives

$$
(y-1)(y+2)^2=(1-2y)^2,
$$

which simplifies to

$$y^3-y^2+4y-5=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

For the transformed roots, $e_1=1$, $e_2=4$, $e_3=5$.

**(b)**

$$p_2=e_1^2-2e_2=1-8=-7. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)**

$$p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=-7-4+15=4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2024-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2024, Q2.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2024-on-11-13}
### 2024 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 3 · 10 marks

<span class="tag">Quartic equation</span><span class="tag">Higher power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The quartic equation $x^4+2x^3-1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.

**(a)** Find a quartic equation whose roots are $\alpha^4,\beta^4,\gamma^4,\delta^4$ and state the value of $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4$. **[5]**

**(b)** Find $\alpha^5+\beta^5+\gamma^5+\delta^5$. **[3]**

**(c)** Find $\alpha^8+\beta^8+\gamma^8+\delta^8$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=x^4$. From the original equation, $2x^3=1-y$. Raising both sides to the fourth power and using $x^{12}=y^3$ gives

$$16y^3=(1-y)^4.$$

Hence

$$y^4-20y^3+6y^2-4y+1=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 M1 A1}$$

Therefore

$$\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4=20. \qquad \text{B1}$$

**(b)** Multiplying the original equation by $x$ and summing over the roots,

$$p_5+2p_4-p_1=0.$$

Since $p_1=-2$,

$$p_5=-2(20)-2=-42. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

**(c)** For the roots $\alpha^4,\beta^4,\gamma^4,\delta^4$, the pairwise sum is $6$. Thus

$$p_8=20^2-2(6)=388. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2024-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2024, Q3; 9231/13/O/N/2024, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2024 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 3 · 10 marks

<span class="tag">Quartic symmetric sums</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

It is given that

$$
\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=2,\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2=3,\qquad
\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3=4.
$$

**(a)** Find $\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\alpha^2\beta+\alpha^2\gamma+\alpha^2\delta
+\beta^2\alpha+\beta^2\gamma+\beta^2\delta\\
&\quad+\gamma^2\alpha+\gamma^2\beta+\gamma^2\delta
+\delta^2\alpha+\delta^2\beta+\delta^2\gamma.
\end{aligned}
\qquad \textbf{[3]}
$$

**(c)** It is given that $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are the roots of

$$6x^4-12x^3+3x^2+2x+6=0.$$

**(i)** Find $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4$. **[3]**

**(ii)** Find $\alpha^5+\beta^5+\gamma^5+\delta^5$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$e_2=\frac{p_1^2-p_2}{2}=\frac{4-3}{2}=\frac12. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(b)** Let the required sum be $T$. Expanding $e_1e_2$ includes every term in $T$ once and each triple product three times, so $e_1e_2=T+3e_3$. Newton's identity gives

$$4=p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=6-1+3e_3,$$

so $e_3=-1/3$. Also

$$e_1e_2=(\text{required sum})+3e_3.$$

Therefore the required sum is

$$2\left(\frac12\right)-3\left(-\frac13\right)=2. \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1}$$

**(c)** The monic equation is

$$x^4-2x^3+\frac12x^2+\frac13x+1=0.$$

**(i)**

$$p_4=2p_3-\frac12p_2-\frac13p_1-4=\frac{11}{6}. \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1}$$

**(ii)**

$$p_5=2p_4-\frac12p_3-\frac13p_2-p_1=-\frac43. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2024-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2024, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2025 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 7 marks

<span class="tag">Cubed-root transformation</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+2x+1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

**(a)** Find a cubic equation whose roots are $\alpha^3-1,\beta^3-1,\gamma^3-1$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find

$$\left(\alpha^3-1\right)^2+\left(\beta^3-1\right)^2+\left(\gamma^3-1\right)^2. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

**(c)** Find

$$\left(\alpha^3-1\right)^3+\left(\beta^3-1\right)^3+\left(\gamma^3-1\right)^3. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=x^3-1$, so $x^3=y+1$. The original equation gives

$$
2x=-(y+2).
$$

Cubing and using $x^3=y+1$,

$$
8(y+1)=-(y+2)^3,
$$

which simplifies to

$$y^3+6y^2+20y+16=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}$$

For the transformed roots, $e_1=-6$, $e_2=20$, $e_3=-16$.

**(b)**

$$p_2=(-6)^2-2(20)=-4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)**

$$p_3=-6(-4)-20(-6)+3(-16)=96. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2025-mj-11-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2025, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2025, Q2.</div>
:::

### 2025 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 3 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Quartic power sums</span><span class="tag">Standard sums</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The quartic equation $x^4+7x^2+3x+22=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.

**(a)** Find $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2$. **[2]**

**(b)** Find $\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4$. **[2]**

**(c)** Use standard results from the list of formulae (MF19) to find

$$
\sum_{r=1}^{10}\left(
(\alpha^2+r)^2+(\beta^2+r)^2+(\gamma^2+r)^2+(\delta^2+r)^2
\right). \qquad \textbf{[5]}
$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since $e_1=0$ and $e_2=7$,

$$p_2=0-2(7)=-14. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(b)** Summing the original equation over the roots,

$$p_4+7p_2+3p_1+88=0,$$

so $p_4=10$. **M1 A1**

**(c)** For each $r$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&(\alpha^2+r)^2+(\beta^2+r)^2+(\gamma^2+r)^2+(\delta^2+r)^2\\
&\qquad=p_4+2rp_2+4r^2
=4r^2-28r+10.
\end{aligned}
\qquad \text{B1 M1 A1FT}
$$

Thus

$$
4\sum_{r=1}^{10}r^2-28\sum_{r=1}^{10}r+100
=4(385)-28(55)+100
=\boxed{100}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}
$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2025-mj-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2025, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 4 · 10 marks

<span class="tag">Symmetric sums</span><span class="tag">Singular matrix</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+bx^2+cx-1=0$, where $b,c$ are constants, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.

It is given that

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\alpha&\beta\\
\alpha&1&\gamma\\
\beta&\gamma&1
\end{pmatrix}
$$

is singular.

**(a)** Show that $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=3$. **[4]**

**(b)** It is given that $\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=3$ and that $b,c$ are positive. Find $b,c$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The determinant is

$$1-\alpha^2-\beta^2-\gamma^2+2\alpha\beta\gamma.$$

Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=1$ and the determinant is zero,

$$\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=1+2=3. \qquad \text{M1 A1 M1 A1}$$

**(b)**

$$3=b^2-2c. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

Summing the original equation over the roots gives

$$3=-3b+bc+3,$$

so $b(c-3)=0$. Since $b>0$, $c=3$. Substitution gives $b=3$. **M1 A1 DM1 A1**

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2025-mj-14"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/14/M/J/2025, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2025 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 4 · 8 marks

<span class="tag">Quartic linear transformation</span><span class="tag">Power sums</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The quartic equation $x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=0$ has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$.

**(a)** Show that a quartic equation with roots $2\alpha+1,2\beta+1,2\gamma+1,2\delta+1$ is

$$y^4-2y^3+4y^2+2y+11=0. \qquad \textbf{[4]}$$

The sum $(2\alpha+1)^n+(2\beta+1)^n+(2\gamma+1)^n+(2\delta+1)^n$ is denoted by $S_n$.

**(b)** Find $S_2$. **[2]**

**(c)** Given that $S_3=-22$, find $S_4$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Put $y=2x+1$, so $x=(y-1)/2$. Substitution and multiplication by $16$ give

$$
(y-1)^4+2(y-1)^3+4(y-1)^2+8(y-1)+16=0,
$$

which simplifies to

$$y^4-2y^3+4y^2+2y+11=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1 A1}$$

For the transformed roots, $e_1=2$ and $e_2=4$.

**(b)**

$$S_2=2^2-2(4)=-4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)** Summing the transformed quartic over its four roots,

$$S_4-2S_3+4S_2+2S_1+44=0.$$

Thus

$$S_4=-76. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2025-on-11-13"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2025, Q4; 9231/13/O/N/2025, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 2 · 8 marks

<span class="tag">Recovering coefficients</span><span class="tag">Fourth power sum</span><span class="tag">★★★★☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$, where $b,c,d$ are constants, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$. It is given that

$$
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2,\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=3,\qquad
\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4=5.
$$

**(a)** Find $b,c$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find $d$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$b=-2. \qquad \text{B1}$$

Also

$$3=(-2)^2-2c,$$

so $c=1/2$. **M1 A1**

**(b)** Let $S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n$. Summing the original cubic over its three roots gives

$$S_3+bS_2+cS_1+3d=0,$$

so

$$S_3=5-3d. \qquad \text{M1 A1FT}$$

Multiplying the original cubic by $x$ and summing over its roots gives

$$S_4+bS_3+cS_2+dS_1=0.$$

Substitution gives

$$5-2(5-3d)+\frac12(3)+2d=0,$$

so

$$d=\frac7{16}. \qquad \text{M1 A1FT A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2025-on-12"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2025, Q2.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card #text-roots-2025-on-14}
### 2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 2 · 9 marks

<span class="tag">Reciprocal relation</span><span class="tag">Unknown coefficients</span><span class="tag">★★★☆☆</span>

The cubic equation $x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0$, where $d\ne0$, has roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ such that

$$\gamma=\frac1\beta.$$

**(a)** Show that

$$\beta+\frac1\beta=d-b. \qquad \textbf{[3]}$$

**(b)** Show also that

$$\beta+\frac1\beta=\frac{1-c}{d}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}$$

**(c)** It is given that $b=3$, $c=-3$ and $d>0$.

**(i)** Find $d$. **[2]**

**(ii)** Find $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Since $\alpha\beta\gamma=-d$ and $\gamma=1/\beta$, $\alpha=-d$. **B1**

**(a)** Using the sum of roots,

$$-d+\beta+\frac1\beta=-b,$$

so

$$\beta+\frac1\beta=d-b. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(b)** Using the sum of pairwise products,

$$-d\beta+1-\frac d\beta=c,$$

which gives

$$\beta+\frac1\beta=\frac{1-c}{d}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

**(c)(i)**

$$d-3=\frac4d,$$

so $d^2-3d-4=0$. Since $d>0$, $d=4$. **M1 A1**

**(c)(ii)**

$$\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=b^2-2c=9+6=15. \qquad \text{M1 A1}$$

</details>

<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="roots-text-2025-on-14"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/14/O/N/2025, Q2.</div>
:::
